---
title: "xenium_nb — QC"
subtitle: "Per-cell QC distributions and QC in tissue, one section per sample"
# Pin the kernel by name, as cluster_report.qmd does. Apptainer bind-mounts $HOME, so
# kernelspecs from ~/.local/share/jupyter/kernels shadow the container's own — quarto's
# default "python3" then resolves to a host env missing the pipeline's packages, and
# every cell fails at import under `error: true` while the render still exits 0.
jupyter: python_spatial
format:
  pptx:
    reference-doc: ouhsc_ppt_template.pptx
    # `#` becomes a Section Header slide, `##` a Title-and-Content slide. Without
    # this pandoc infers the level from the headings present, so adding the first
    # `#` would silently demote every `##` to a bullet.
    slide-level: 2
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  # Keep rendering when a cell raises: one sample's panel erroring leaves an error slide
  # in its own section instead of taking the whole deck down. The cost is that a
  # genuinely broken cell yields an error slide and an exit code of 0 — read the slides,
  # not just the exit status.
  error: true
---

```{python}
# | tags: [setup]
import textwrap
import traceback
from functools import partial
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import scanpy as sc
import spatialdata
import spatialdata_plot  # noqa: F401 — registers the .pl accessor on SpatialData
from IPython.display import display, Markdown
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm, Normalize


class SafeLogNorm(LogNorm):
    """LogNorm that does not re-derive its limits once both are given.

    Works around an incompatibility between spatialdata_plot and matplotlib 3.11, not
    anything about this data. spatialdata_plot calls norm.autoscale_None() with the 2D
    label array, and matplotlib's generated LogNorm.autoscale_None transforms its input
    unconditionally — even when vmin and vmax are already set — through a LogTransform
    that only accepts (N, 1). The result is
    "ValueError: Input values must have shape (N, 1) or (1,)" and no plot at all.

    Short-circuiting when both limits are known keeps the log mapping and never reaches
    the failing transform. Delete this once the two libraries agree again; a plain
    LogNorm is the intended call.
    """

    def autoscale_None(self, A):
        if self.vmin is None or self.vmax is None:
            super().autoscale_None(A)

# The reference template is 16:9 at 10 x 5.625in; leave room for a slide title.
FIGSIZE = (9.0, 4.3)
# Inches reserved beside the in-tissue plots for their colorbar, which sits outside
# the axes and would otherwise be cropped by tight_layout.
LEGEND_WIDTH = 1.4

# Deck-wide figure settings, set once here rather than per call so every slide matches.
#
# 400 dpi is chosen from the display, not from the print convention that usually
# supplies this number. These figures are 9in wide on a 10in slide, so they span 90% of
# it: a 4K screen puts 3456 pixels across that span, which needs 384 dpi. 300 (the
# offset-print number) covers 1440p and a page printed at 100%; 200 covers a 1080p
# projector and nothing above it. Matplotlib's default is 100, which is why the text
# looked soft — 7pt glyphs are about ten pixels tall before PowerPoint scales them up.
#
# The cost is roughly 4x the file size of 100 dpi, which is ~800 KB of figures for a
# two-sample deck. It grows with the cohort AND with the point count of the tissue
# scatters, so a cohort of whole-slide samples is the case where this needs revisiting.
plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 400,
    "savefig.dpi": 400,
    "font.size": 8.5,
    "axes.labelsize": 8.5,
    "axes.titlesize": 8.5,
    "xtick.labelsize": 7.5,
    "ytick.labelsize": 7.5,
    "figure.titlesize": 10.5,
})

# Histogram bar fill, and the ink used for the median rule and its label. One fill for
# every panel: the four metrics are small multiples of the same measurement, not four
# series, so varying the hue would imply a distinction that does not exist.
BAR_FILL = "#7BA3CC"
ANNOTATION_INK = "#333333"
GRID_INK = "#E6E6E6"

# Every raw zarr is staged into this notebook's working directory by the Nextflow
# process, so globbing is the whole input contract — no params to pass or drift.
#
# These are create_sdata's zarrs, NOT cluster_sdata's: nothing here has been filtered
# yet, which is the point. Reading this deck off clustered zarrs would show only the
# cells that survived the min_counts cut, with the discarded tail already gone — so the
# distributions would look clean no matter how much was thrown away.
ZARRS = sorted(Path(".").glob("*.zarr"))
if not ZARRS:
    raise FileNotFoundError("No .zarr directories staged next to the notebook.")

# Every per-cell QC column this deck shows, as (obs column, axis label, scale). All come
# straight from the zarr — create_sdata annotates the counts and ratios, the Xenium reader
# supplies the areas, nucleus count and segmentation method from cells.parquet. This deck
# derives nothing.
#
# This deck is exploratory: every metric appears on every plot type it can, so the whole
# panel can be looked at once and the uninformative ones dropped afterwards. That is why
# the list is long and why nothing here is packed to save space.
#
# The scale is what makes one list able to drive three different plot types. It picks the
# histogram's binning and axis, and the tissue panel's colour norm, because those are the
# same decision asked twice. The four kinds are genuinely different, not a log flag:
#
#   log          counts and areas spanning decades. Zeros cannot be drawn and are counted.
#   linear       bounded ratios and percentages. Zeros are real values and are kept — for
#                pct_control they are 87% of cells, so dropping them would empty the panel.
#   count        small integers (0–15). Binned on integer edges so each bar is one value;
#                60 logspace bins over 4 distinct values is mostly empty bars.
#   categorical  no bins and no colourbar at all — a bar chart of category counts, and a
#                discrete palette with a legend in tissue.
METRICS = [
    ("transcript_counts", "Transcripts per cell", "log"),
    ("n_genes_by_transcripts", "Genes per cell", "log"),
    ("cell_area", "Cell area (µm²)", "log"),
    ("nucleus_area", "Nucleus area (µm²)", "log"),
    ("nucleus_ratio", "Nucleus / cell area", "linear"),
    ("transcripts_per_gene", "Transcripts per gene", "linear"),
    ("pct_control", "Control transcripts (%)", "linear"),
    ("control_counts", "Control transcripts per cell", "count"),
    ("nucleus_count", "Nuclei per cell", "count"),
    ("segmentation_method", "Segmentation method", "categorical"),
    ("pct_transcripts_in_top_5_genes", "Transcripts in top 5 genes (%)", "linear"),
    ("pct_transcripts_in_top_10_genes", "Transcripts in top 10 genes (%)", "linear"),
    ("pct_transcripts_in_top_20_genes", "Transcripts in top 20 genes (%)", "linear"),
    ("pct_transcripts_in_top_50_genes", "Transcripts in top 50 genes (%)", "linear"),
]

# Histogram panels per slide. The metrics are small multiples of one measurement rather
# than a figure each, so they stay gridded even though the tissue and scatter slides do
# not — a 2x2 is still readable at slide size, where a quarter-slide tissue panel is not.
HIST_PANELS = 4

# Every obs column this deck reads, checked against each zarr in the loop below. All of
# them come from create_sdata or the Xenium reader; none is derived here. Listing them in
# one place means a zarr that predates a column fails on the first sample with the column
# named, rather than several slides later inside whichever panel happened to want it.
REQUIRED_OBS = [col for col, _, _ in METRICS] + ["sample"]


# ── Slides ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# One function per slide, each emitting its own heading, caption, and figure. The
# per-sample loop below is then literally a list of the slides in the order they appear,
# and adding or reordering one is a line there rather than a block edit. Keeping the
# caption next to the figure it describes is the other half of it — the two are edited
# together far more often than either is edited alone.


def qc_histogram_slide(sdata, sample, metrics):
    """Slide: this sample's per-cell QC, one histogram per metric.

    Hand-rolled rather than a library call, because scanpy has no histogram function.
    The other slides use sc.pl / spatialdata_plot and let those size their own marks.

    A 2x2 grid over one HIST_PANELS-sized chunk of METRICS, so adding or dropping a
    metric there changes the slides without touching this function. Leftover axes are
    removed rather than hidden — a hidden axes still reserves its cell under tight_layout
    and squeezes the real panels into a fraction of the slide.

    The binning is chosen by each metric's scale rather than shared, because the four
    kinds fail differently on each other's treatment:

      log     logspace bins, so bars are uniform width on the log axis instead of
              crowding into the left of each decade. Zeros cannot be drawn at all.
      linear  even bins over the observed range, and zeros are KEPT. They are ordinary
              values for a bounded ratio or a percentage — pct_control is 0 for 87% of
              cells, so borrowing the log panels' zero-dropping would empty the panel and
              report the emptying as a footnote.
      count   one bar per integer, on half-offset edges so each bar is centred on its
              value. nucleus_count takes four distinct values; 60 bins over it is 56
              empty bars and four spikes too thin to see.

    Cells fall off a panel two different ways, and both are counted beside the median
    rather than left to disappear — they are exactly the cells a QC deck must not hide.
    A value of zero cannot be drawn on a LOG axis (transcript_counts reaches 0 on real
    data). A value that was never measured is NaN: the reader leaves nucleus_area NaN,
    not 0, for a cell segmented without a nucleus, which is 70 of 21,724 on one ROI, and
    create_sdata's division carries that NaN into nucleus_ratio. The two are reported
    separately because they mean different things — "this cell had none" versus "this
    cell was not measured". Plotting an unmeasured cell at 0 would file it among
    genuinely cytoplasm-heavy ones.

    A categorical metric gets horizontal bars instead: there is no median to mark, no
    binning to choose, and the category names are sentences, so they belong on the axis
    that has room for them. It shares the slide with the numeric panels rather than
    taking its own, since it is the same question about the same cells.

    The styling is deliberate on three points. Bars carry a white separator, because at
    60 bins a solid fill reads as one mass and the gap is what lets neighbours be told
    apart. The left spine is dropped in favour of a recessive horizontal grid, since bar
    heights are read against gridlines and the axis line itself carries no information.
    And the median is labelled where it stands rather than in a panel title, so the
    number sits next to the rule it describes.
    """
    display(Markdown("## Per-cell QC distributions"))
    display(Markdown(
        "Distributions of "
        + ", ".join(label.lower() for _, label, _ in metrics)
        + " across all cells in this sample, before any filtering. The dashed line marks "
        "each median. Counts and areas are on log axes, where cells at zero cannot be "
        "drawn; ratios and percentages are on linear axes, where zero is plotted like any "
        "other value. Cells with no nucleus have no nucleus area or ratio to draw. Cells "
        "that cannot be drawn are counted beside the median instead."
    ))

    table = sdata.tables["table"]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=FIGSIZE, squeeze=False)
    for ax, (col, label, scale) in zip(axes.ravel(), metrics):
        if scale == "categorical":
            # Sorted so the axis reads as a ranking; the names are long enough that
            # alphabetical order would give the eye nothing to hold onto.
            counts = table.obs[col].value_counts().sort_values()
            ax.barh(range(len(counts)), counts.to_numpy(),
                    color=BAR_FILL, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.25)
            ax.set_yticks(range(len(counts)))
            # Wrapped, not truncated: these names differ in their tail (which stain), so
            # cutting them short makes the categories indistinguishable.
            ax.set_yticklabels(["\n".join(textwrap.wrap(str(c), 34)) for c in counts.index],
                               fontsize=5.5)
            ax.set_xlabel("Cells")
            ax.set_title(label, fontsize=8.5)
            ax.grid(axis="x", color=GRID_INK, lw=0.6)
            ax.set_axisbelow(True)
            ax.tick_params(length=0)
            ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)
            continue

        raw = table.obs[col].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        finite = raw[np.isfinite(raw)]

        if scale == "log":
            drawn = finite[finite > 0]
            bins = np.logspace(np.log10(drawn.min()), np.log10(drawn.max()), 60)
        elif scale == "count":
            drawn = finite
            # Half-offset integer edges, so each bar covers exactly one value.
            bins = np.arange(finite.min(), finite.max() + 2) - 0.5
        else:
            drawn = finite
            bins = np.linspace(finite.min(), finite.max(), 60)

        ax.hist(drawn, bins=bins, color=BAR_FILL, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.25)
        if scale == "log":
            ax.set_xscale("log")

        # Median over every MEASURED value, not just the plotted ones: dropping zeros is
        # a drawing constraint, and letting it move the median would misreport the sample.
        # Unmeasured cells are excluded, since they have no value to rank.
        median = float(np.median(finite))
        ax.axvline(median, color=ANNOTATION_INK, lw=1.0, ls="--")

        # Ratios and percentages need decimals; counts and areas do not, and a median of
        # "226.00" transcripts reads as a precision the metric does not have.
        note = f"median {median:,.0f}" if scale != "linear" else f"median {median:,.2f}"
        # Only counted where zeros were actually dropped, i.e. on a log axis. On a linear
        # or count panel they are drawn, so there is nothing to report.
        n_zero = len(finite) - len(drawn)
        if n_zero:
            note += f" · {n_zero:,} at zero"
        n_missing = len(raw) - len(finite)
        if n_missing:
            note += f" · {n_missing:,} not measured"
        # Anchored to the median in data coords but the top of the axes in fraction
        # coords, so the label tracks the rule horizontally and stays clear of the bars.
        ax.annotate(note, xy=(median, 1), xycoords=("data", "axes fraction"),
                    xytext=(4, -11), textcoords="offset points",
                    color=ANNOTATION_INK, fontsize=7.5)

        ax.set_xlabel(label)
        ax.set_ylabel("Cells")
        ax.grid(axis="y", color=GRID_INK, lw=0.6)
        ax.set_axisbelow(True)
        ax.tick_params(length=0)
        ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False)

    for ax in axes.ravel()[len(metrics):]:
        fig.delaxes(ax)

    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {table.n_obs:,} cells", x=0.01, ha="left")
    fig.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def transcripts_vs_genes_slide(sdata, sample, color, label, scale):
    """Slide: genes detected against transcript count, coloured by one obs column.

    The joint view the histogram slide cannot give: the two metrics are strongly coupled,
    so a cell that is unusual in the pair — many transcripts spread over few genes, or the
    reverse — sits off the main arm while looking ordinary in either margin alone.

    One slide per colour rather than a row of panels, so each scatter gets the whole
    slide. The geometry is identical every time; what changes is which cells light up.
    That is a lot of near-identical slides at METRICS' current length, and deliberately
    so — the deck is being read to decide which colours are worth keeping, which cannot
    be decided from the ones that were left out.

    Three of the colours are functions of the two axes rather than new dimensions: the
    axes themselves, and transcripts_per_gene, which on log axes is distance from the
    diagonal. They are kept because re-encoding position is not the same as showing
    nothing — the eye judges perpendicular distance poorly on log axes, and an axis
    recoloured onto itself is the reference the others are read against. The area,
    control and segmentation colours are the ones carrying genuinely independent
    information: they say whether off-arm cells are also unusual in size, in background,
    or in how they were segmented.

    A categorical colour is passed through unchanged — scanpy draws a discrete palette
    with a legend instead of a colourbar when the column is categorical, so nothing here
    branches on it. It does require the column to BE categorical, which is scanpy's own
    sanitize_anndata step on an object column, not something this deck does.

    Drawn by sc.pl.scatter with NO ax= passed. That matters: given an axes, scanpy has
    nowhere to put the colourbar and draws it on top of the data. Left to build its own
    figure it allocates a proper colourbar axes, so the size comes from
    rcParams["figure.figsize"] here instead of a figsize argument.

    Log on both axes for the same reason the histograms use it: counts span orders of
    magnitude, and on linear axes the whole cohort collapses into the bottom-left corner.
    The scale is applied afterwards because sc.pl.scatter has no log option; matplotlib
    then drops any cell at zero on either axis, so those are counted from the data and
    reported in the title rather than vanishing silently.

    Colour is left on its full range for now. Both area columns have long right tails
    (cell_area reaches ~1,180 µm² against a median of 45), so most cells sit at the dark
    end — clipping or a log norm is the open question, deliberately not decided here.
    """
    display(Markdown(f"## Transcripts vs genes — {label}"))
    display(Markdown(
        "One point per cell: transcript count against the number of genes detected in "
        f"that cell, both on log axes, coloured by {label.lower()}. Cells at zero on "
        "either axis cannot be drawn on a log axis and are counted in the title instead."
    ))

    table = sdata.tables["table"]
    # figsize via rc_context because scanpy builds the figure itself; see the docstring.
    with plt.rc_context({"figure.figsize": FIGSIZE}):
        sc.pl.scatter(
            table,
            x="transcript_counts",
            y="n_genes_by_transcripts",
            color=color,
            show=False,
        )

    fig = plt.gcf()
    ax = fig.axes[0]
    ax.set_xscale("log")
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    # scanpy labels the axes with the raw obs keys; restate them in the deck's wording.
    ax.set_xlabel("Transcripts per cell")
    ax.set_ylabel("Genes detected per cell")
    ax.set_title(label)
    ax.grid(color=GRID_INK, lw=0.6)
    ax.set_axisbelow(True)
    ax.tick_params(length=0)

    x = table.obs["transcript_counts"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    y = table.obs["n_genes_by_transcripts"].to_numpy(dtype=float)
    n_dropped = int(((x <= 0) | (y <= 0)).sum())

    title = f"{sample} · {table.n_obs:,} cells"
    if n_dropped:
        title += f" · {n_dropped:,} at zero"
    fig.suptitle(title, x=0.01, ha="left")
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)


def qc_tissue_labels_slide(sdata, sample, color, label, scale):
    """Slide: the cell segmentation, coloured by one QC metric.

    Drawn with spatialdata_plot's render_labels, which paints each cell's own segmented
    footprint rather than a marker at its centroid. That is the whole reason to use it:
    a scatter needs a marker size and there is no non-arbitrary one. A constant does not
    travel between a 2,000 µm ROI and a whole slide; deriving it from cell spacing works
    but still leaves a coverage factor that is pure taste. Painting the mask retires the
    question — a cell is exactly as big as it is.

    Note it is NOT smaller on disk at slide scale, which a quick test on a small canvas
    suggests it should be: at this figure size and dpi the label panels land within a few
    percent of the scatter they replaced (~3.3 MB each). The saving only appears on a
    small, low-dpi canvas where contiguous regions compress well; blown up to a full
    slide there is enough boundary detail to erase it.

    render_labels, not render_shapes, though both can draw real cell outlines. The table
    annotates `cell_labels`, so labels work with no schema change, while colouring
    `cell_boundaries` by a QC column needs a second table keyed on cell_id. At this
    magnification a cell is about two points across, so the polygons' extra fidelity is
    not visible — it would only pay off zoomed in.

    One metric per slide, each with its own norm and colourbar. Sharing a scale across
    metrics is not an option even in principle here — genes top out near 2,400 on these
    ROIs against ~10,600 transcripts and 3% control — but the reason for a whole slide
    each is that these panels are read for spatial STRUCTURE, and a quarter-slide panel of
    a 21k-cell ROI is too small to see any. It makes for a long deck, which is the
    intended trade while the metrics are still being chosen.

    The norm follows the metric's scale, and getting it wrong is not cosmetic: a log norm
    over pct_control (0–3%) or nucleus_ratio (0–1) spends the whole ramp below 1 and
    masks the 87% of cells sitting at exactly 0, so the panel reads as empty tissue. A
    categorical metric takes no norm and no colormap at all — spatialdata_plot assigns a
    discrete palette and draws a legend instead of a colourbar.

    Zeros on a LOG panel are handled through the colormap rather than by clipping the
    data: a log norm masks non-positive values, and a masked pixel takes the colormap's
    "bad" colour, which defaults to transparent — those cells would silently vanish from
    the panel that exists to locate them. Painting `bad` with the bottom of the ramp keeps
    them visible without altering a value. Linear panels need none of this.

    The figure is sized here rather than by the library, because nothing in it can choose
    an orientation from the tissue's shape. A fixed size wastes the slide on anything that
    is not 2:1, since equal aspect is non-negotiable for tissue and a tall section renders
    as a sliver down the middle of a wide figure. These ROIs run both ways — one a 3:1
    strip, the other a 1:2.2 block — so the panel is fitted to each sample's own aspect,
    touching whichever edge of the slide's plot box binds first.

    Axis ticks are hidden rather than labelled. spatialdata's `global` frame for a Xenium
    read is in PIXELS — cell_labels maps to it with an identity transform while the
    boundary polygons carry a 4.7059 scale — so the numbers on these axes are not µm and
    would be actively misleading. The squidpy version carried a µm scale bar instead;
    restoring one here needs the pixel size, which nothing in the object records where
    this function can reach it.
    """
    display(Markdown(f"## In tissue — {label}"))
    display(Markdown(
        f"Each cell drawn at its segmented shape and position, coloured by {label.lower()}"
        + (" on a log colour scale. Cells at zero are painted the bottom of the ramp."
           if scale == "log" else
           " on a discrete palette, one colour per category." if scale == "categorical"
           else " on a linear colour scale.")
        + " The panel is at tissue proportions with an equal aspect."
    ))

    table = sdata.tables["table"]

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(FIGSIZE[0], FIGSIZE[1]))

    # Solid fill, no outline: at this magnification a cell is a couple of points across,
    # so an outline would be most of it and the default alpha only muddies the colour it
    # is there to show.
    render = dict(color=color, fill_alpha=1.0, outline_alpha=0.0)
    if scale == "log":
        values = table.obs[color].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        positive = values[np.isfinite(values) & (values > 0)]
        cmap = plt.get_cmap("viridis").copy()
        # See the docstring: masked (non-positive) pixels would otherwise be transparent.
        cmap.set_bad(cmap(0.0))
        render |= {"cmap": cmap,
                   "norm": SafeLogNorm(vmin=positive.min(), vmax=positive.max())}
    elif scale != "categorical":
        values = table.obs[color].to_numpy(dtype=float)
        render |= {"cmap": "viridis",
                   "norm": Normalize(vmin=np.nanmin(values), vmax=np.nanmax(values))}

    sdata.pl.render_labels("cell_labels", **render).pl.show(ax=ax, title="")

    # Lay the panel out by hand, and do NOT call tight_layout here — it is what left a
    # band of empty slide beside every tissue panel. spatialdata_plot attaches its
    # colourbar as a free-standing axes that tight_layout does not know about, so
    # tight_layout expands the main axes from 77% to 92% of the figure width, straight
    # under the colourbar. The axes holds an equal aspect, so it cannot use that width and
    # instead centres itself in the oversized box, putting the slack on its left.
    #
    # The aspect is read back from the drawn limits rather than computed from
    # obsm["spatial"]: the two agree here (2.8568 either way, since the label raster is
    # cropped to the cells), but the limits are what the axes will actually honour.
    aspect = abs(np.ptp(ax.get_xlim()) / np.ptp(ax.get_ylim()))
    # Margins in inches. The top one carries both the panel title and the suptitle, and is
    # sized for the two of them stacked — a tall sample makes a narrow figure, where the
    # suptitle wraps closer to the panel and the two would otherwise touch.
    left, top, bottom = 0.06, 0.60, 0.06
    panel_w = FIGSIZE[0] - left - LEGEND_WIDTH
    panel_h = panel_w / aspect
    # A tall sample binds on height instead, and would otherwise run off the slide.
    if panel_h + top + bottom > FIGSIZE[1]:
        panel_h = FIGSIZE[1] - top - bottom
        panel_w = panel_h * aspect
    fig_w, fig_h = left + panel_w + LEGEND_WIDTH, top + panel_h + bottom
    fig.set_size_inches(fig_w, fig_h)
    ax.set_position([left / fig_w, bottom / fig_h, panel_w / fig_w, panel_h / fig_h])
    # Re-seat the colourbar beside the panel it belongs to, since it was placed against
    # the figure the library saw rather than the one this slide ends up with. A
    # categorical metric has a legend instead and no second axes to move.
    for cax in fig.axes[1:]:
        cax.set_position([(left + panel_w + 0.12) / fig_w, bottom / fig_h,
                          0.16 / fig_w, panel_h / fig_h])

    ax.set_title(label)
    ax.set_xlabel("")
    ax.set_ylabel("")
    # See the docstring: these axes are in pixels, not µm.
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])

    # No tight_layout: see the positioning block above.
    fig.suptitle(f"{sample} · {table.n_obs:,} cells", x=0.01, ha="left")
    plt.show()
    plt.close(fig)
```

```{python}
# One `# <sample>` section per sample, driven by the staged zarrs rather than a hardcoded
# block each: the cohort changes, and a hardcoded list silently omits a new sample while
# raising KeyError on a removed one.
#
# Each sample's AnnData is dropped as soon as its slides are drawn, so a cohort's worth
# of obs frames is never co-resident.
#
# Every heading here and in the slide functions is emitted with display(Markdown(...))
# from an ORDINARY cell, NOT under `output: asis`. Under asis everything a cell displays
# concatenates into one raw markdown stream: the figure lands between the blocks and
# leaves the next heading not starting its own line, so pandoc prints a literal "## ..."
# as text and drops the image entirely. display(Markdown) does not hit it — each call
# emits its own complete block, and each figure ends with plt.show() so it lands
# between them.
for path in ZARRS:
    # Load the sample as one SpatialData and hand that to every slide, reaching for
    # .tables["table"] where a slide wants the annotations. One object, loaded once, in
    # the pipeline's own artifact type — no second representation to keep in step.
    #
    # Only labels and tables: the deck draws the segmentation and reads obs, and nothing
    # else. Images stay out because it plots none of them.
    #
    # This does read X into memory, which the previous read_lazy loader avoided. The
    # trade is worth it — 17 MB for a 21k-cell ROI, and the lazy version needed
    # adata.obs/var .to_memory() calls anyway, because read_lazy returns them as xarray
    # Dataset2D and every scanpy/squidpy plot fails on that (scverse/anndata#981).
    # Loading plainly costs some memory and removes a workaround. Revisit if a cohort of
    # whole-slide samples makes X the binding constraint; it is per sample and dropped
    # below, so the ceiling is one sample's matrix, not the cohort's.
    sdata = spatialdata.read_zarr(path, selection=("labels", "tables"))
    table = sdata.tables["table"]

    # This deck computes no QC metric of its own, and has no fallbacks. A report that
    # derives a metric is a second definition of it, and the two drift without anything
    # saying so; a fallback is that second definition wearing a disguise, letting a stale
    # cohort render a deck whose numbers came from outside the pipeline. Failing here
    # names the fix, which is to re-run create_sdata.
    #
    # Outside the per-sample try below, deliberately: a missing column means the whole
    # cohort came from a create_sdata that predates it, so failing the render outright is
    # more useful than a traceback slide repeated once per sample.
    missing = [c for c in REQUIRED_OBS if c not in table.obs.columns]
    if missing:
        raise KeyError(
            f"{Path(path).name}: obs is missing {missing}. These come from create_sdata "
            "— re-run it over this sample rather than deriving them here."
        )

    # obs["sample"] is written by create_sdata, so the sample id comes from the object
    # rather than the staged path — which is a meaningless sample1.zarr, since the
    # process stages every zarr under an indexed name.
    sample = str(table.obs["sample"].iloc[0])

    display(Markdown(f"# {sample}"))

    # The slides, in the order they appear, each caught independently. Built from METRICS
    # rather than written out, so a metric added there appears on all three plot types at
    # once and nothing can be added to one and forgotten on another: the histogram grids
    # in chunks of HIST_PANELS, then the scatter and the tissue panel once per metric.
    #
    # The scatter skips the categorical metric only because sc.pl.scatter is the one call
    # here whose colour handling this deck does not control; every numeric metric gets all
    # three views, including the two that ARE the scatter's axes — see that slide's
    # docstring for why the degenerate colours are kept rather than filtered out.
    slides = [partial(qc_histogram_slide, metrics=METRICS[i:i + HIST_PANELS])
              for i in range(0, len(METRICS), HIST_PANELS)]
    slides += [partial(transcripts_vs_genes_slide, color=col, label=label, scale=scale)
               for col, label, scale in METRICS if scale != "categorical"]
    slides += [partial(qc_tissue_labels_slide, color=col, label=label, scale=scale)
               for col, label, scale in METRICS]

    # This loop is a single cell, so anything raising without being caught aborts the cell
    # and drops every LATER sample from the deck too — with the render still exiting 0
    # under `error: true`.
    #
    # Per slide rather than per sample because these slides share nothing: each reads the
    # same adata and draws its own figure, so one failing says nothing about the others.
    # Catching
    # here also puts the traceback under the failed slide's OWN title, since every slide
    # function emits its heading before it plots — which names the broken slide instead
    # of leaving a traceback loose in the section.
    #
    # (A deck whose slides read shared derived state — a correlation matrix feeding three
    # slides, say — wants one try around that computation instead: if it fails, every
    # slide downstream of it is meaningless and should be skipped together.)
    for slide in slides:
        try:
            slide(sdata, sample)
        except Exception:
            # close(), not close(fig): the slide raised before reaching its own close,
            # so the half-built figure is still open and unreachable from here.
            plt.close()
            display(Markdown(f"```\n{traceback.format_exc()}\n```"))

    del sdata, table
```
